reviews.reasoning: The span opens on the declarative praise formula “Great is Yahweh, and greatly to be praised” (web:Ps.48.1; oshb:Ps.48.2 גָּ֘ד֤וֹל יְהוָ֣ה וּמְהֻלָּ֣ל מְאֹ֑ד בְּעִ֥יר אֱ֝לֹהֵ֗ינוּ הַר קָדְשֽׁוֹ), continues through the description of Zion's beauty and location (web:Ps.48.2), and closes on “God has shown himself in her citadels as a refuge” (web:Ps.48.3). The next strophe opens with the explanatory particle pair כִּֽי הִנֵּ֣ה ("for behold," oshb:Ps.48.5), a clean shift from third-person description to narrative report -- a genuine tier-1 discourse-frame boundary confirmed directly from source bytes. Tiling within the cluster's Psalm 48 rows is exact (WEB 1-14, no gaps or overlaps). The device_notes genre labels (shir, mizmor, livnei_qorach) match psalm_device_inventory.json's superscription entry for psalm 48 exactly, and the title dual-cite (web:Ps.48.0 = oshb:Ps.48.1) is correct under the shift+1 rule. No stronger rival seam was found one verse away; confidence high is warranted, and the single-sentence rejected_alternative is well targeted.

Opens on כִּֽי הִנֵּ֣ה הַ֭מְּלָכִים ("for behold, the kings," oshb:Ps.48.5) narrating the assault, the panic simile of a woman in travail (48:6), and the east-wind destruction of the Tarshish fleet, closing on the confirmation formula “as we have heard, so we have seen” (web:Ps.48.8) sealed by Selah at oshb:Ps.48.9 -- confirmed present in pmarks_Ps.json (71-verse inventory). Selah functions only as corroboration of the close, not the driver; the actual close is the confirmation-formula content, consistent with book policy. The cross-reference to the shared "we have heard" motif at web:Ps.44.1 (explicitly disclosed as "a separate parent composition") is an accurate, correctly dual-cited intertextual note, not a merge or boundary claim, and is properly mirrored in boundary_evidence_refs. All quoted WEB text is verbatim. Confidence high is supported.

Opens on the first-person-plural meditative verb pair דִּמִּ֣ינוּ אֱלֹהִ֣ים חַסְדֶּ֑ךָ ("we have thought about your loving kindness, God," oshb:Ps.48.10), a genuine address-mode shift from third-person report to direct second-person speech to God, corroborated (not driven) by the preceding strophe's Selah. The strophe closes on the Zion/Judah wish at 48:11, which still addresses God in the same verse ("because of your judgments") even while naming Zion and Judah in the third person -- a genuinely soft seam before the imperative cluster opening at 48:12 (סֹ֣בּוּ צִ֭יּוֹן, "walk about Zion," addressed to the community rather than to God). The device_notes candidly flag this as a seam "without a new disclosure-object marker," and the medium confidence rating is an honest, well-calibrated response to that genuine softness rather than an overclaim. A verse-by-verse check of 48:9-12 found no stronger rival seam.

Opens on the plural imperative pair סֹ֣בּוּ צִ֭יּוֹן ("walk about Zion," oshb:Ps.48.13) addressing the community, and closes the psalm on the confession כִּ֤י זֶ֨ה אֱלֹהִ֣ים אֱ֭לֹהֵינוּ עוֹלָ֣ם וָעֶ֑ד ה֖וּא יְנַהֲגֵ֣נוּ עַל מֽוּת ("for this God is our God forever and ever," oshb:Ps.48.15) rather than a baruch/amen doxology. The device_notes' disclaimer that this is not one of the book's four doxology seams (41|42, 72, 89|90, 106) is accurate against psalm_device_inventory.json's book_boundary_doxologies entries, and correctly keeps unit_type at strophe rather than coda. Tiling with the preceding three rows is exact (WEB 1-14, no gaps or overlaps). Confidence high is supported by the clean imperative-cluster opener and the confession close.

The universal-audience summons opening (“Hear this, all you peoples…”, web:Ps.49.1) is a genuine tier-1 opener signature, and extending the row through 49:4 to capture the wisdom-instruction performative is a defensible literary-form judgment -- the mashal/riddle word pair is a recognized wisdom-opening convention. The genre-label device_notes (mizmor, lamnatseach, livnei_qorach) are accurate against the inventory, and tiling plus dual-cite arithmetic (49.0=49.1, 49.4=49.5, forward cites to 49.12/49.20) are correct and properly mirrored. However the row's own citation for the mashal/riddle pairing misidentifies the Hebrew word for "riddle" (see the challenge below), which weakens the stated warrant for treating 49:4 as belonging with the opening summons rather than with the argument beginning at 49:5.

challenges.claim: The row glosses oshb:Ps.49.5's בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר as "(riddle)" in both rationale and observed_substrate_signals, but that word means "with/on the harp" (kinnor, a lyre; cf. Gen.4.21, 1Sam.16.16), not riddle.
challenges.evidence: Byte-collated word split of oshb:Ps.49.5 (tier=byte via collate.py): אַטֶּ֣ה לְמָשָׁ֣ל אָזְנִ֑י אֶפְתַּ֥ח בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר חִידָתִֽי. The sixth and final word, חִידָתִֽי ("my riddle"), is the verse's actual chidah/riddle term and pairs with לְמָשָׁ֣ל ("to a proverb", word 2) for the mashal/chidah wisdom-opening convention the row is arguing for; the fifth word בְּ֝כִנּ֗וֹר that the row cites as "(riddle)" is the instrumental phrase "with/on the harp" and never means riddle. The row's own WEB quotation “I will solve my riddle on the harp” (web:Ps.49.4) shows the correct English pairing, but the row's inline Hebrew gloss is bound to the wrong lexeme in the same verse, in both places the quote is used.

reviews.reasoning: The rhetorical-question opener (49:5, “why should I fear”) and the death/wealth argument through 49:10 read as one continuous discourse with no addressee shift, and the refrain at 49:11-12 gives a legitimate tier-1 close; the "death/wealth pivot" rejected_alternative is well argued and its single-sentence form is compliant. The refrain-comparison claim between oshb:Ps.49.13 and oshb:Ps.49.21 understates the actual byte-level variance (see the challenge below); this is a precision defect in the supporting evidence, not in the span or the underlying boundary warrant -- the refrain still closes the unit even though it is a near-repeat rather than an exact one, as the row itself already discloses.

challenges.claim: The row characterizes the oshb:Ps.49.13/oshb:Ps.49.21 refrain variance as a single substituted verb, but byte comparison shows three points of difference, not one.
challenges.evidence: Byte-collated (tier=byte) word split: oshb:Ps.49.13 = וְאָדָ֣ם | בִּ֭יקָר | בַּל | יָלִ֑ין | נִמְשַׁ֖ל | כַּבְּהֵמ֣וֹת | נִדְמֽוּ; oshb:Ps.49.21 = אָדָ֣ם | בִּ֭יקָר | וְלֹ֣א | יָבִ֑ין | נִמְשַׁ֖ל | כַּבְּהֵמ֣וֹת | נִדְמֽוּ. Word 1 drops the vav-conjunctive (וְאָדָ֣ם → אָדָ֣ם), word 3 swaps the negator (בַּל → וְלֹ֣א), and word 4 swaps the verb (יָלִ֑ין → יָבִ֑ין); only words 2 and 5-7 are identical. The row's own "not byte-identical" disclosure is correct in spirit, but "the medial verb… substituted" undercounts the variance by two tokens.

reviews.reasoning: The second meditation panel is real and the refrain at 49:19-20 does close it, so the overall span and unit_type are defensible in principle. But the row's rejected_alternative asserts that no addressee or speech-frame shift accompanies either Selah in the span, and that claim is both textually wrong and internally inconsistent with the row's own rationale -- see the primary challenge below. The secondary, lower-severity issue is the same refrain-variance imprecision already identified at the parallel seam in the neighboring strophe, repeated here by cross-reference.

challenges.claim: The rejected_alternative's claim that "no addressee or speech-frame shift accompanies either Selah here" is false and directly contradicts the row's own rationale, which describes the verse right after the second Selah as a "pivot to direct exhortation."
challenges.evidence: MT Ps.49.16 (=web:Ps.49.15, tier=byte) closes on the first-person-suffixed verb יִקָּחֵ֣נִי ("he will receive me") immediately before סֶֽלָה (Selah): אַךְ אֱלֹהִ֗ים יִפְדֶּ֣ה נַ֭פְשִׁי מִֽיַּד שְׁא֑וֹל כִּ֖י יִקָּחֵ֣נִי סֶֽלָה. MT Ps.49.17 (=web:Ps.49.16, tier=byte) opens אַל תִּ֭ירָא ("do not fear," a 2ms negative address) immediately after that Selah: אַל תִּ֭ירָא כִּֽי יַעֲשִׁ֣ר אִ֑ישׁ כִּֽי יִ֝רְבֶּה כְּב֣וֹד בֵּיתֽוֹ. This is a direct second-person address opening right where the rejected_alternative claims no addressee shift exists -- and the row's own rationale independently names this exact transition a "pivot to direct exhortation" (its description of web:Ps.49.16). The Selah-marked "13-15 | 16-20" rival split therefore has independent, non-selah tier-1 support (an addressee/speech-frame change) that the row's stated warrant incorrectly forecloses; the "high" confidence rating inherits the same defect, since a live, textually-grounded rival is denied rather than weighed.
